title: Kaikeyi's boons
hook: a king spends the whole night arguing with his own promise

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kaikeyi's boons, asked. The king swore by Rama, and she claimed two old gifts: Bharata crowned, Rama to the forest. Did you hear a whole question before saying yes? Today, the longest night in Ayodhya. Day five hundred twenty-one.

It's deep in the night in Kaikeyi's room. The king of Ayodhya, who commands armies, is on the floor beside his queen, trying to find a way out of something he swore a few hours ago. He tries one door, then another, then the first one again. Valmiki doesn't hurry this night. He lets it run, speech after speech, the way a sleepless night runs. And through all of it, Kaikeyi gives him one answer.
screen: `DEEP IN THE NIGHT.` → `THE KING, ON THE FLOOR.` → `ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: When he hears the two boons, the king faints. When he comes to, he tries everything. He pleads: what has Rama done to you? You've praised him yourself; he honors you like his own mother. He reasons: the people will call me a fool, a king ruled by a woman. Kausalya will be shattered. And Bharata himself, the king says, will never accept a throne taken this way. He rages, and says terrible things. Then he falls at her feet and begs. Kaikeyi doesn't move. And her answer is not just stubbornness. She argues from the thing the king is proudest of: his truthfulness. You gave your word, she says. You swore with the gods as witnesses. She reminds him of old kings famous for keeping promises at any cost: King Shibi, who gave his own flesh to a hawk to save a dove that had come to him for shelter, and King Alarka, who gave away his eyes when a brahmin asked for them. If you break your word, she says, you'll be the king who broke his word. Here is the knot at the center of the Ayodhya Kanda. The word is satya, truth, and it means more than not lying. It means your word holding, being as good as a thing done. Dasharatha has built his whole life on satya. Now it's being used against the son he loves. He can't break his promise without breaking himself, and he can't keep it without breaking Rama. The text says he begged the night itself not to end, so the morning would never come. But morning comes.
screen: `THE KING PLEADS, REASONS, RAGES.` · `KAIKEYI ANSWERS: YOU GAVE YOUR WORD.` · `SHIBI AND THE DOVE, ALARKA'S EYES.` · `SATYA: A WORD THAT HOLDS.` · then, large: `BUT MORNING COMES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind something you've promised that's become hard to keep. You don't have to solve it. Just feel the two pulls at once: the wish to keep your word, and the wish to be free of it. Let both be there. Breathe in with one, breathe out with the other, and let the breath hold them side by side. The bell holds the time.
Kaikeyi's boons, defended. The king begs all night, and Kaikeyi holds him to satya, the truth of his own sworn word.
Your line: Kaikeyi's boons. Today, notice one promise you keep easily, and how little it costs you to keep it. Day five hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In the Ramayana, satya, truthfulness, is the king's proudest virtue, and this night is its hard case: a true word that brings grief.

fork.setup: you're Kaikeyi. the king is at your feet, begging you to let the boons go. what do you say?
options: you swore; a king who breaks his word is no king.
fine, ask Rama what he wants.
fork.reveal: she holds him to satya, his sworn word, and names Shibi and Alarka, kings who kept their promises at any cost.

original.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, what is real, a word that holds. the virtue Dasharatha can't give up.

trapdoor: what you thought: the king could simply cancel the boons.
what it means: breaking his sworn word would break satya, the truth his whole reign stands on.
what a scholar hears: Kaikeyi's appeal to Shibi and Alarka uses the king's own ideal against him, and the text lets both pulls stand: satya, and a father's love.

Editor review (2026-10-01): rewrote the hook (it told the listener what their sleepless nights are like, called Dasharatha 'the most powerful man in the kingdom', and counted 'several chapters'); softened the king's line about Rama and Kaikeyi to 'honors you like his own mother' (confirm the exact comparison in Ayodhya 12); removed the sat etymology, 'one of the most often named virtues', 'retold in many homes' and 'commentators still argue'; carry no longer tells the listener to give thanks.
